CHILD KIDNAPPINGS

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate the recent spate of child kidnappings - what are the motives, what are the solutions and ask if children have just become another commodity traded in the underworld?

Unique Selling Point:
- RELEVANT WITH THE FESTIVE SEASON UPON US
- SPATE OF KIDNAPPINGS AND ATTEMPTED KIDNAPPINGS
- OPPORTUNITY TO DO AN AWARENESS PIECE


Summary:
A spate of kidnappings targetting small children across South Africa have parents on high alert.

Motives ranging from ransom to parental abductions and even muthi – we explore the driving forces putting kids at risk and highlight what parents should do in these cases.


Further information:
THE SOUTH AFRICAN KIDNAPPING SITUATION
On statistic that is often used in South Africa is that a child goes missing every 5 hours - this figure would be higher, but kidnappings are not always reported to the police, and when children are found, these cases are not included in those statistics.

While most kidnappings in South Africa are associated with ransoms and sometimes kidnappers hold their captives longer to demand more money from victims’ relatives or associates.

The high kidnapping rate in South Africa is attributed to the high rate of corruption and high crime rate in this country. South Africa has a weak judicial system and a history of social and political instability. Owing to a large number of kidnappings that occur, the police in South Africa are unable to investigate every case to the best of their ability.

EXPERT – MARCEL VAN DER WATT
Marcel van der Watt is attached to the department of police practice at Unisa. He is an ex-Hawks investigator and performs a variety of local and international roles in the field of combating human trafficking and organised crime.

He explains that there is a disconnect between the reality of child abductions in communities and what the police statistics reflect. Van der Watt believes children have become yet another commodity traded on the black market.

The motives for these abductions vary – but the danger remains the same – Van der Watt says his research shows there is a definite increase in these cases.

MOTIVES

Muthi Kidnappings
Small children are kidnapped for body parts used in muthi.

Revenge Kidnappings
Where the assailants are knowns to the family – children are kidnapped to settle a score.

Parental Abductions
The rise in the family breakup and divorce rates and the ease of international travel have led to an increase in parental kidnappings. This scenario plays out when one custodial parent must return their own child to their ex-spouse in terms of a divorce arrangement.

This is kidnapping, it is a criminal offence and must be dealt with accordingly, especially where young children are involved, and the children are kept away from the lawful custodial parent for an extended period.

Distraction Attempted Kidnappings
There has been a spate of kidnappings specifically in Middelburg where petty criminals are grabbing kids out of cars to distract drivers allowing their accomplices to steal valuables from the car – often the child is dropped and the would-be kidnapper makes a run for it. We have footage of this of an incident like this.

Small Ransom Random Kidnappings
This is a relatively new trend in South Africa. It seems modern technology has paved the way for an increase in this dangerous crime. Cell phones, EFT’s and eWallets allow kidnappers to communicate easily from anywhere, to get the money quickly and remotely and then to disappear without a trace. The anonymity of the crime makes random kidnapping attractive to criminals.

The modus operandi is simple; identify the victim, force the victim into a vehicle, tie up individual and then call the helpless abductee’s loved ones to extort ransom money.

Investigators have identified some common elements with this type of abduction:
• The ransom demanded is affordable, less than R 10 000, which makes it possible for the abductee’s family or friends to pay the ransom quickly;
• The abductee’s cell phone is involved, making the entire experience even more terrifying as the family initially think that their child is just calling and get caught completely off guard when the kidnapper announces what has happened to their child this is literally every parents’ worst nightmare;
• The payment must be made into an eWallet or similar digital service, so it is immediately available, secured, and cannot be stopped or easily traced.

High-value Kidnappings
In these cases the captives are usually held for long periods of times. There is a lot of negotiation that goes on often with professional hostage negotiators behind the scenes.

SOLUTIONS: FACEBOOK’S AMBER ALERT
Facebook has an initiative that will deliver AMBER Alerts to people’s News Feeds in targeted search areas after a child has been abducted – this has been used internationally and will now be introduced for the time on the continent in South Africa this December.

These alerts, which include photographs and other details about the missing child, are shown on mobile and desktop. People can share the alert with friends and link directly to SAPS’ missing child poster.

The chances of finding a missing child increase when more people are on the lookout, especially in the critical first hours. Facebook’s goal is to help get these alerts out quickly to the people who are in the best position to help.

The initiative is formally being launched in December.

CASE STUDIES TO INCLUDE
* I HAVE A LIST OF AT LEAST 14 CASES SINCE AUG 2018 THAT HAVE BEEN IN THE MEDIA

Amy-Leigh – Vanderbijl Park – September 2019
NOT AN INTERVIEW – JUST REFERENCE THE INCIDENT

Brackenfell Incident – November 2019
A four-year old girl, was playing in the garden with an 8 year old friend while here parents were inside. A man walked up to them, grabbed the 4 year old and started walking away – the 8 year old screamed and tried to pull the younger girl back – the would-be kidnapper dropped the child and ran off. Media reported that there was footage – but not of the incident – just a suspicious car driving in and out of the area.

Middelburg Incident – November 2019
There is footage. This area in Middelburg has been plagued by thieves stealing valuables out of cars. In the clip, you can see a man coming up along side the passenger side and grabbing the two year old from the back window. The little boy’s older brother jumps out and chases the man screaming and shouting. The man then drops the little boy and runs off. It’s believed this MO is meant to distract the driver long enough for the thieves to steal valuables out of the car – we don’t think it’s to kidnap the kids.

HOW TO DO IT
• We can film dramatisations
• We can use the video clip from Middelburg, I have at least one other of an attempted kidnapping
• I don’t think it’s worth going to Cape Town for the attempted kidnapping, there is also no footage.
• I don’t know if it’s worth going to Middleburg either.
• I think we can get away with the experts and a clever device of the different incidents, dramatizations and the clips.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: Child Abductions are rampant. Kids are at risk all over South Africa – with at least two children going missing every single day.

Watch this video from an incident in Middelburg. Keep an eye on the passenger side of the vehicle.

Just like that in 10 seconds a child was almost taken.

LIZETTE: I didn't // cross my mind he will take my kids. I mean you never think anybody will take your kids. And there's the next moment. It just happened

VO: Lizette van Niekerk’s 9 year old son, Nathan, jumped out after his little brother Raygan was almost snatched, causing the man to run away.

LIZETTE: I don't want to think about it because he would have maybe ran off with him. He had a knife with him. So. I don't know what his plan was.

VO: The video went viral with South Africans alarmed by this new crime trend.

LINK: Was it a distraction for petty thieves? Kidnap for ransom? Was it an abduction for muthi? The reality is we can’t say for sure, but we do know without a doubt – is that children, are not safe. They are vulnerable targets for exploitation.

MARCEL: These a variety of reasons which really is just camouflaged in current day South Africa with all of these structural inequalities and systems of violence that we are faced with.

VO: More often than not the people behind abductions are known to their victims. Marcel van der Watt is a former hawks-investigator and specialist human trafficking researcher.

MARCEL: // we are often fixated by the idea that it takes a village to raise a child but we often forget that these are predators and traffickers // they often have an insider's perspective on issues of vulnerability and the movement of families

VO: In September, a case in Vanderbijlpark, south of Joburg made headlines – when 6-year-old Amy-Leigh de Jager was kidnapped outside her school. While a R2 million ransom was initially demanded, the kidnappers lost their nerve and dumped her on a street just 19 hours later.

Four suspects were arrested and charged Bafokeng Molemohi, Laetitia Nel, Pieter Jacobus van Zyl and Tharina Human, who was a teacher at Amy-Leigh’s school.

This is a voice note from Human’s father:

UPSOUND NEWS24:


VO: Modus operandi are adapted to different scenarios - the methods used to adbuct children range from taking them forcefully, to deceit and cohersion.

In a social experiment done at a park in America, parents insisted their children knew of stranger danger and would never walk off with someone unknown to them. But watch as a stranger, manages to walk away with children - in under a minute.

Despite what parents think they’ve taught their children, kids under the age of seven are extremely vulnerable to kidnapping - even more so if the child is socially confident explains Psychologist Ilze Alberts.

ILZE: // It's so easy to lure a child away. You just need to know what is the language of a child what is important for a child.

VO: Criminals zone in and take advantage of children’s innocence and trusting nature.

ILZE: They have not developed All those masks in front of them. Those layers and layers of protection and they still believe that the world is a good place. And especially the grown ups are good and there to help them and to look after them. INT1 M1

VO: Irrespective of the motive, vulnerability is the common denominator when it comes to abdcutions, explains Van der Watt.

MARCEL: // whether it's an Amy-leigh that's being kidnapped for a small ransom amount or whether it's a seven year old Thandeka who has been lured to a flat and does online sexual services effectively coming down to child pornography // our children are predisposed it's that vulnerability and the toxic mix of all of these things that really creates this enabling environment

VO: When a child goes missing, every second counts – quick reaction is crucial. Major General Bafana Linda heads up the police’s Family Violence, Child Protection and Sexual Offences Division.

This December the South African Police Service has launched a new initiative that will incorporate targeted social media alerts.

GEN LINDA: // We are partnering. With Facebook. // where we have an Amber Alert that will be assisting us in terms of. The recovery of children or tracing an investment of the missing children within a particular area in a very short space of time.

VO: The initiative successfully runs in 21 countries worldwide – South Africa will be the first on the continent to implement Amber Alerts.

A missing person report will be generated by the national board of missing persons. It will then be disseminated by Facebook’s 24 hour command centre, to users within a 160 kilometer radius of where the child went missing.

GEN LINDA: //Child protection is everyone’s business. INT1 M22 // You don't have to wait 24 hours. // we want to utilize the time that a child goes missing. With better opportunities to recover a child to while still unharmed INT1 M9

VO: But kidnappers feed off fear. The threat of harm, is usually enough to manipulate parents into not contacting the police and paying ransom instead.

A recent case in Joburg started off as a mugging but then turned into a small ransom kidnapping. Armed with guns and knives, opportunistic thugs decided to hold three young men hostage demanding ransom from their parents.

UPSOUND CALL:
DAD: are you gonna definitely release him and let them walk back to the car with his phone?
KIDNAPPER: Obvious, I want what I want
DAD: Please, please don’t hurt him, I’m paying you the money like we agreed.

VO: The money was sent via multiple eWallet transactions The cash was then withdrawn from an ATM – and the victims were released after being held hostage for about four hours.

While sophisticated syndicates focus on kidnapping for high value ransoms, where the victims are usually adults - a new wave of low level criminals are setting their sites on RANDOMLY kidnapping minors for small ransoms.

DUDLEY: Everybody is a target not only the rich and people that can pay millions It's opportunistic.

VO: Dudley Booysen is a risk solutions consultant that is part of a network of investigators handling kidnap & ransom cases in South Africa.

DUDLEY: // the latest trends we start seeing less and less money so it's easier to get hold of. I mean as a parent as easily pay 10000 Rand then hundreds of millions of rand.

VO: These criminals don’t risk a cash drop off – the more tech-savvy kidnappers could demand payment in crypto-currencies, while others simply want a quick transfer banking solution, where cash can be transferred to a cellphone number that’s usually not RICA-ed.

CLAIRE: Paying the ransom. Are we not encouraging them to do well again.
DUDLEY: Absolutely. That's unfortunately the scenario that it is creating a vicious circle - that creates a market for it.

GEN LINDA: Remember that it is no guarantee that after you have delivered the ransom that the child be released you might deliver that in some end. They will ask for some more Money as you cooperate with them.

VO: The driving forces behind abductions vary – sometimes it’s not even for ransom – it could be a parental kidnapping in custody disputes or in more sinisters cases for human trafficking.

CLAIRE: Is there a demand for our children.
MARCEL: Absolutely// this is fundamentally enabled and perpetuated by the demand for commercial sex and cheap labor. And that's where children often becomes the commodified objects that are being recruited bought and sold.

VO: In some cases syndicates even place orders for specific types of children

DUDLEY: There will be a syndicate that ask for a specific age, specific look alike and then they will get kidnapped

VO: The scenario is different to the usual kidnapping operation explains Booysen.

DUDLEY: //They wont to make contact with no one. They don’t want a ransom and sadly that In those cases it's very unlikely that that kid will get found.

LINK: Abducting children has become a profitable income stream for criminals. The cops are seemingly slow to follow up on leads meaning the chance of an arrest or jail time is slim to none – making it a near perfect crime with big yield and little risk.

MARCEL: // They are emboldened. // they know that you rarely get caught. You rarely get arrested and even the risk even much far lower than you know getting convicted.

VO: The police unfortunately play a reactionary role. Major General Linda emphasises that the first priority is to get the victim back as quickly as possible and unharmed.

Alberts believes its vital for parents to be pro-active in safeguarding their children.

ILZE: Tell them it’s wrong to walk away

VO: While the police’s Amber Alert programme will go a long way in finding abducted children, Van der Watt warns that pro-active solutions are needed.

MARCEL: // it's a systemic problem// And if we fail with a systemic approach it's inevitable that the problem, The dangers the risks will simply be amplified. //INT1 M27

PROMO 1

Four suspects were arrested and charged Bafokeng Molemohi, Laetitia Nel, Pieter Jacobus van Zyl and Tharina Human, who was a teacher at Amy-Leigh’s school. This is a voice note from Human’s father: UPSOUND NEWS24: VO: Modus operandi are adapted to different scenarios - the methods used to adbuct children range from taking them forcefully, to deceit and cohersion. In a social experiment done at a park in America, parents insisted their children knew of stranger danger and would never walk off with someone unknown to them. But watch as a stranger, manages to walk away with children - in under a minute. Despite what parents think they’ve taught their children, kids under the age of seven are extremely vulnerable to kidnapping - even more so if the child is socially confident explains Psychologist Ilze Alberts. ILZE: // It's so easy to lure a child away. You just need to know what is the language of a child what is important for a child. VO: Criminals zone in and take advantage of children’s innocence and trusting nature. ILZE: They have not developed All those masks in front of them. Those layers and layers of protection and they still believe that the world is a good place. And especially the grown ups are good and there to help them and to look after them. INT1 M1 VO: Irrespective of the motive, vulnerability is the common denominator when it comes to abdcutions, explains Van der Watt. MARCEL: // whether it's an Amy-leigh that's being kidnapped for a small ransom amount or whether it's a seven year old Thandeka who has been lured to a flat and does online sexual services effectively coming down to child pornography // our children are predisposed it's that vulnerability and the toxic mix of all of these things that really creates this enabling environment VO: When a child goes missing, every second counts – quick reaction is crucial. Major General Bafana Linda heads up the police’s Family Violence, Child Protection and Sexual Offences Division. This December the South African Police Service has launched a new initiative that will incorporate targeted social media alerts. GEN LINDA: // We are partnering. With Facebook. // where we have an Amber Alert that will be assisting us in terms of. The recovery of children or tracing an investment of the missing children within a particular area in a very short space of time. VO: The initiative successfully runs in 21 countries worldwide – South Africa will be the first on the continent to implement Amber Alerts. A missing person report will be generated by the national board of missing persons. It will then be disseminated by Facebook’s 24 hour command centre, to users within a 160 kilometer radius of where the child went missing. GEN LINDA: //Child protection is everyone’s business. INT1 M22 // You don't have to wait 24 hours. // we want to utilize the time that a child goes missing. With better opportunities to recover a child to while still unharmed INT1 M9 VO: But kidnappers feed off fear. The threat of harm, is usually enough to manipulate parents into not contacting the police and paying ransom instead. A recent case in Joburg started off as a mugging but then turned into a small ransom kidnapping. Armed with guns and knives, opportunistic thugs decided to hold three young men hostage demanding ransom from their parents. UPSOUND CALL: DAD: are you gonna definitely release him and let them walk back to the car with his phone? KIDNAPPER: Obvious, I want what I want DAD: Please, please don’t hurt him, I’m paying you the money like we agreed. VO: The money was sent via multiple eWallet transactions The cash was then withdrawn from an ATM – and the victims were released after being held hostage for about four hours. While sophisticated syndicates focus on kidnapping for high value ransoms, where the victims are usually adults - a new wave of low level criminals are setting their sites on RANDOMLY kidnapping minors for small ransoms. DUDLEY: Everybody is a target not only the rich and people that can pay millions It's opportunistic. VO: Dudley Booysen is a risk solutions consultant that is part of a network of investigators handling kidnap & ransom cases in South Africa. DUDLEY: // the latest trends we start seeing less and less money so it's easier to get hold of. I mean as a parent as easily pay 10000 Rand then hundreds of millions of rand. VO: These criminals don’t risk a cash drop off – the more tech-savvy kidnappers could demand payment in crypto-currencies, while others simply want a quick transfer banking solution, where cash can be transferred to a cellphone number that’s usually not RICA-ed. CLAIRE: Paying the ransom. Are we not encouraging them to do well again. DUDLEY: Absolutely. That's unfortunately the scenario that it is creating a vicious circle - that creates a market for it. GEN LINDA: Remember that it is no guarantee that after you have delivered the ransom that the child be released you might deliver that in some end. They will ask for some more Money as you cooperate with them. VO: The driving forces behind abductions vary – sometimes it’s not even for ransom – it could be a parental kidnapping in custody disputes or in more sinisters cases for human trafficking. CLAIRE: Is there a demand for our children. MARCEL: Absolutely// this is fundamentally enabled and perpetuated by the demand for commercial sex and cheap labor. And that's where children often becomes the commodified objects that are being recruited bought and sold. VO: In some cases syndicates even place orders for specific types of children DUDLEY: There will be a syndicate that ask for a specific age, specific look alike and then they will get kidnapped VO: The scenario is different to the usual kidnapping operation explains Booysen. DUDLEY: //They wont to make contact with no one. They don’t want a ransom and sadly that In those cases it's very unlikely that that kid will get found. LINK: Abducting children has become a profitable income stream for criminals. The cops are seemingly slow to follow up on leads meaning the chance of an arrest or jail time is slim to none – making it a near perfect crime with big yield and little risk. MARCEL: // They are emboldened. // they know that you rarely get caught. You rarely get arrested and even the risk even much far lower than you know getting convicted. VO: The police unfortunately play a reactionary role. Major General Linda emphasises that the first priority is to get the victim back as quickly as possible and unharmed. Alberts believes its vital for parents to be pro-active in safeguarding their children. ILZE: Tell them it’s wrong to walk away VO: While the police’s Amber Alert programme will go a long way in finding abducted children, Van der Watt warns that pro-active solutions are needed. metadata.Summary: A spate of kidnappings targetting small children across South Africa have parents on high alert. Motives ranging from ransom to parental abductions and even muthi – we explore the driving forces putting kids at risk and highlight what parents should do in these cases.
metadata.Further information: THE SOUTH AFRICAN KIDNAPPING SITUATION On statistic that is often used in South Africa is that a child goes missing every 5 hours - this figure would be higher, but kidnappings are not always reported to the police, and when children are found, these cases are not included in those statistics. While most kidnappings in South Africa are associated with ransoms and sometimes kidnappers hold their captives longer to demand more money from victims’ relatives or associates. The high kidnapping rate in South Africa is attributed to the high rate of corruption and high crime rate in this country. South Africa has a weak judicial system and a history of social and political instability. Owing to a large number of kidnappings that occur, the police in South Africa are unable to investigate every case to the best of their ability. EXPERT – MARCEL VAN DER WATT Marcel van der Watt is attached to the department of police practice at Unisa. He is an ex-Hawks investigator and performs a variety of local and international roles in the field of combating human trafficking and organised crime. He explains that there is a disconnect between the reality of child abductions in communities and what the police statistics reflect. Van der Watt believes children have become yet another commodity traded on the black market. The motives for these abductions vary – but the danger remains the same – Van der Watt says his research shows there is a definite increase in these cases. MOTIVES Muthi Kidnappings Small children are kidnapped for body parts used in muthi. Revenge Kidnappings Where the assailants are knowns to the family – children are kidnapped to settle a score. Parental Abductions The rise in the family breakup and divorce rates and the ease of international travel have led to an increase in parental kidnappings. This scenario plays out when one custodial parent must return their own child to their ex-spouse in terms of a divorce arrangement. This is kidnapping, it is a criminal offence and must be dealt with accordingly, especially where young children are involved, and the children are kept away from the lawful custodial parent for an extended period. Distraction Attempted Kidnappings There has been a spate of kidnappings specifically in Middelburg where petty criminals are grabbing kids out of cars to distract drivers allowing their accomplices to steal valuables from the car – often the child is dropped and the would-be kidnapper makes a run for it. We have footage of this of an incident like this. Small Ransom Random Kidnappings This is a relatively new trend in South Africa. It seems modern technology has paved the way for an increase in this dangerous crime. Cell phones, EFT’s and eWallets allow kidnappers to communicate easily from anywhere, to get the money quickly and remotely and then to disappear without a trace. The anonymity of the crime makes random kidnapping attractive to criminals. The modus operandi is simple; identify the victim, force the victim into a vehicle, tie up individual and then call the helpless abductee’s loved ones to extort ransom money. Investigators have identified some common elements with this type of abduction: • The ransom demanded is affordable, less than R 10 000, which makes it possible for the abductee’s family or friends to pay the ransom quickly; • The abductee’s cell phone is involved, making the entire experience even more terrifying as the family initially think that their child is just calling and get caught completely off guard when the kidnapper announces what has happened to their child this is literally every parents’ worst nightmare; • The payment must be made into an eWallet or similar digital service, so it is immediately available, secured, and cannot be stopped or easily traced. High-value Kidnappings In these cases the captives are usually held for long periods of times. There is a lot of negotiation that goes on often with professional hostage negotiators behind the scenes. SOLUTIONS: FACEBOOK’S AMBER ALERT Facebook has an initiative that will deliver AMBER Alerts to people’s News Feeds in targeted search areas after a child has been abducted – this has been used internationally and will now be introduced for the time on the continent in South Africa this December. These alerts, which include photographs and other details about the missing child, are shown on mobile and desktop. People can share the alert with friends and link directly to SAPS’ missing child poster. The chances of finding a missing child increase when more people are on the lookout, especially in the critical first hours. Facebook’s goal is to help get these alerts out quickly to the people who are in the best position to help. The initiative is formally being launched in December. CASE STUDIES TO INCLUDE * I HAVE A LIST OF AT LEAST 14 CASES SINCE AUG 2018 THAT HAVE BEEN IN THE MEDIA Amy-Leigh – Vanderbijl Park – September 2019 NOT AN INTERVIEW – JUST REFERENCE THE INCIDENT Brackenfell Incident – November 2019 A four-year old girl, was playing in the garden with an 8 year old friend while here parents were inside. A man walked up to them, grabbed the 4 year old and started walking away – the 8 year old screamed and tried to pull the younger girl back – the would-be kidnapper dropped the child and ran off. Media reported that there was footage – but not of the incident – just a suspicious car driving in and out of the area. Middelburg Incident – November 2019 There is footage. This area in Middelburg has been plagued by thieves stealing valuables out of cars. In the clip, you can see a man coming up along side the passenger side and grabbing the two year old from the back window. The little boy’s older brother jumps out and chases the man screaming and shouting. The man then drops the little boy and runs off. It’s believed this MO is meant to distract the driver long enough for the thieves to steal valuables out of the car – we don’t think it’s to kidnap the kids. HOW TO DO IT • We can film dramatisations • We can use the video clip from Middelburg, I have at least one other of an attempted kidnapping • I don’t think it’s worth going to Cape Town for the attempted kidnapping, there is also no footage. • I don’t know if it’s worth going to Middleburg either. • I think we can get away with the experts and a clever device of the different incidents, dramatizations and the clips.
